explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus doesn't pick either one. He says, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him.” The disciples handed Him a two-option question, and He answered with a third door. I've been handed plenty of questions with no good choices, so I respect that move.

That's one of the two choices the disciples offered, so I see why it's tempting. But Jesus doesn't take it. He says, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned…” The man was blind from birth, and Jesus doesn't pin it on him.

The disciples did put that option on the table, friend. Jesus passes on it, though. He says, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him.” So nobody gets the blame here, and the focus moves to what God is about to display.

Yes, baker! Jesus says, “While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” He says it right after talking about night coming, when no one can work. Light and night in the same breath, and it all fits. I know what a sliver of light means after years in the dark.

Jesus did say that one, just somewhere else. It's in John 6:35, when He says, “I am the bread of life.” Here in chapter 9, though, He's talking about daytime and night, so the name that fits is the light of the world. Good catch on a real saying of His, wrong stop.

That's a real name Jesus uses for Himself. In John 10:11 He says, “I am the good shepherd.” But in this moment He's just finished talking about daytime and night. So He calls Himself the light of the world.

True, friend. Jesus tells him to go wash in the Pool of Siloam, and the man goes, washes and comes back seeing. No arguing, no stalling. A man blind from birth walks off, and a different man walks back.

The text says otherwise, baker. Jesus tells him to go wash in the Pool of Siloam, and the man went and washed, and came back seeing. So the trip works out exactly the way Jesus said. He went off blind and returned with his sight.

That's the one, baker! While some say it's him and others say it's not, the man keeps saying, “I am the one.” He's got the best proof in the whole argument, because he's the guy. When everyone's debating who you are, it helps to just keep saying it.

Ha, the twin theory keeps going in this version. But the man never claims to be anybody's brother. The text says he kept saying, “I am the one.” He's the same man who used to sit and beg, and he says so.
Nope, this guy has no doubt about who he is. The neighbors are the ones going back and forth. The man keeps saying, “I am the one.” He knows exactly who he is, even with a brand new view.

I see why you'd think so, but it's the other way around. The neighbors ask, “Where is He?” and the man answers, “I do not know.” He knows what happened to him and he knows the name Jesus, but he can't point to where Jesus is right now.

That's right, friend. When they ask where Jesus is, he answers, “I do not know.” He can tell them everything about what happened to his eyes, but not where Jesus has gone. A man will always be honest about what he doesn't know, and I like that about him.
Yes, baker. John 9:14 says the day Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes was a Sabbath. That's a small detail with big consequences. The Pharisees pick it up in a hurry, as you'll see.
The text doesn't call it a feast day. John 9:14 says it was a Sabbath. That one detail is what gets the Pharisees talking, so it's worth holding on to.
Not a fasting day, friend. John 9:14 tells us it was a Sabbath. Nothing in the passage mentions fasting. Keep your eye on that Sabbath, because it matters in what comes next.
Not quite, baker. The man doesn't refuse anything. When the Pharisees ask how he received his sight, he answers, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and now I can see.” He tells them straight.
That's right, baker. He doesn't hold anything back. He tells the Pharisees, “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and now I can see.” He gives them the facts and he's not shy about it.

explanations.answer: How can a sinful man perform such signs
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker! Others say, “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” That's a sharp question, because it points at what Jesus actually did. The Pharisees are split, and it all starts with a Sabbath and some mud.

explanations.answer: Why would God heal on that day
explanations.explanation: That sounds like it could be in there, but it isn't. The text has the other Pharisees ask, “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” They look at the sign itself and ask how someone sinful could do it. Nobody in the passage asks why God would heal on that day.

explanations.answer: Who gave this man His authority
explanations.explanation: Good question, but nobody asks it here. These Pharisees ask, “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” Their question is about the signs, not about authority. That one line is what splits the room.

You got it, baker. Asked what he says about Jesus, since it was his eyes that were opened, the man replies, “He is a prophet.” Notice he's already moving from calling Him a man named Jesus to something more. He's thinking it through, and he's doing it out loud.

That's what some others say, but not him. The man replies, “He is a prophet.” He's the one whose eyes were opened, so his answer carries weight. Calling Jesus a sinner comes later from the Jews, in verse 24.

He did say he didn't know where Jesus was, but he doesn't call Him a stranger. Asked what he says about Jesus, he answers, “He is a prophet.” That's a lot more than a stranger. He's got a different view of this man now.
That's right, baker. His parents say, “We know he is our son…” Even with leaders breathing down their necks, that part they say plainly. A parent knows their own.
Yes, friend. They say he “was born blind.” They back up what he's been saying from the start. His eyes were really closed all his life, and they know it.
The parents don't call him a servant. They say, “We know he is our son…” It's a family question and they answer it as family.
Close in sound, but no, baker. The parents say he was born blind. Nothing in the passage says he was deaf. His eyes are the whole story here.
Not lame, friend. His parents say he was born blind. This man could walk fine, since Jesus sent him to the pool and he went. His eyes are what changed.
True, baker. His parents say, “But how he can now see or who opened his eyes, we do not know.” They'll confirm he's their son and that he was born blind. Past that, they stop.

The text says the opposite, friend. His parents answer, “But how he can now see or who opened his eyes, we do not know.” They're only willing to vouch for the parts they're sure of. The rest they hand back to him.

explanations.answer: They are afraid of the Jews
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says, “His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jews.” They'd heard what would happen to anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ. It's a pressure moment, and I think anybody who's felt that knot in their stomach understands.

explanations.answer: They are angry with their son
explanations.explanation: The text never says they're angry with him. It says they spoke up this way because they were afraid of the Jews. Their words are “Ask him. He is old enough to speak for himself.” That's fear talking, not anger.

The text gives a different reason. It says, “His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jews.” Nothing says they were trying to shield Jesus. They were looking at what could happen to them.

explanations.answer: They would be put out of the synagogue
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. John 9:22 says the Jews “had already determined that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue.” The synagogue was the community's gathering place, so being put out was a real loss. That's why the parents choose their words so carefully.

explanations.answer: They would be sent out of the city
explanations.explanation: That sounds serious, but it's not what the text says. John 9:22 says anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. The threat was about the synagogue, not the city.

explanations.answer: They would have to pay a fine
explanations.explanation: No fine is mentioned, friend. John 9:22 says the Jews decided anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. Money doesn't come into it at all.

explanations.answer: I was blind but now I see
explanations.explanation: That's the line, baker! He says, “Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!” He doesn't pretend to know more than he does. He stands on what he knows, and nobody can argue him off it.
He doesn't say that here. He says, “Whether He is a sinner I do not know.” What he does say he knows for sure is, “I was blind, but now I see!” He sticks to what he's lived.

His parents didn't claim that. They said they didn't know how he could now see or who opened his eyes. The man's point is his own: “I was blind, but now I see!” He's not leaning on anyone else's word.
He doesn't, baker. He says, “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again?” That's no retelling. He asks them a question instead.

That's right, friend. He says, “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again?” Then he asks if they also want to become Jesus' disciples. I'd tell you I've never had a moment that bold, but I once argued with a mixing bowl.
That's right, baker. They say, “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses.” Moses was Israel's leader, the one they say God spoke to. They put themselves on one side and the man on the other.
Abraham, Israel's famous forefather, is a good guess, but he isn't who they name. They say, “We are disciples of Moses.” Moses was Israel's leader. That's the name they claim.
Elijah was a prophet of Israel, but they don't mention him here. The Jews say, “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses.” Moses was Israel's leader, and that's the name they hold up.

Nope, he doesn't back down at all. He answers, “That is remarkable indeed!” and keeps going. He points out that they don't know where Jesus is from, and yet Jesus opened his eyes. He's just getting warmed up.

That's right, baker. Instead of backing down, he says, “That is remarkable indeed!” Then he lays out his point: they don't know where Jesus is from, and yet He opened his eyes. A man who sat and begged is now out-arguing the experts, and I'm here for it.
The man says the very opposite, baker. He tells them, “Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind.” This had no track record. That's why it's such a big deal.

That's right, friend. He says, “Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind.” He's telling them this has never been heard of. It's the strongest evidence in the room, and he's wearing it.
Yes, baker. He says, “If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.” That's the end of his argument, and it's tight. He saw what happened, and he followed it to the only place it leads.
Egypt is a nation from Israel's history, but it's not in his sentence. He says, “If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.” His whole point is about where this power comes from.
Babylon was another nation from Israel's history, but it doesn't show up here. The man says, “If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.” The word he lands on is God.

That's what happens, baker. Right after he makes his case, they answer, “You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?” And they threw him out. It's a heavy moment, and I think this one stings.
No apology happens here, friend. They reply, “You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?” And they threw him out. It goes the other direction.
The Jews don't go looking for Jesus. They throw the man out. Jesus is the one who goes looking, in verse 35. It's His move, not theirs.

explanations.answer: He asks who the Son of Man is
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. He says, “Who is He, Sir? Tell me so that I may believe in Him.” He's ready to believe, he just needs to know who. It's an honest question, and it gets an answer.

explanations.answer: He asks Him for a sign
explanations.explanation: He doesn't ask for a sign. He says, “Who is He, Sir? Tell me so that I may believe in Him.” He's already had his eyes opened, so what he wants is to know who he's believing in.
He doesn't say that, friend. He asks, “Who is He, Sir? Tell me so that I may believe in Him.” That's a man leaning toward belief, just looking for the name.
True, baker. He says, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped Jesus. He started this day begging by the road, and now he's kneeling in worship. What a day.
The text says it plainly, friend. He says, “Lord, I believe,” and he worshiped Jesus. No hesitation. He answers, and then he worships.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, “For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind.” And we just watched a blind man see. The words and the story line up.
That's not the word Jesus uses here, friend. He says, “…so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind.” Given the man we just watched, that word fits.
Not the word Jesus uses, baker. He says, “…so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind.” He's talking about seeing and blindness.

That's the question, baker. Some of the Pharisees with Him ask, “Are we blind too?” They heard what He said about those who see becoming blind, and it landed on them. That's a question people ask when a statement hits close to home.

That worry shows up earlier, from the Jews talking to the man. Here the Pharisees ask Jesus, “Are we blind too?” They heard what He said about the blind and those who see. That's the part they respond to.
That question isn't in this passage, friend. The Pharisees with Jesus ask, “Are we blind too?” They're reacting to what He just said about seeing and blindness.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, “If you were blind, you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains.” They said they could see, and He takes them at their word. It's a serious line, and Jesus leaves it there.
That's not what Jesus says here, friend. He says, “But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains.” He ties their guilt to their claim to see.

No, baker. Jesus doesn't point at anyone's parents here. He says, “But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains.” Back in verse 2 the disciples wondered about the man's parents, and Jesus said then that neither the man nor his parents sinned. Here He speaks only about those who claim they see.
